Daniel’s central move—shifting from “LLM as obedient tool-user” to “LLM as an interface that proactively *studies the user* and proposes new interaction schemes”—quietly assumes that the best interface is one where the system performs much of the conceptual work the user would otherwise do (modeling the domain, mapping intentions to tools, and even discovering workflows). That’s plausible, but it also risks collapsing two distinct goals: *reducing cognitive overhead* vs *preserving user agency and skill formation*. In a flute-tutoring setting, that tension is acute: the learner is not merely trying to “achieve outputs” but to internalize technique, self-monitoring, and musical judgment. A LAUI that is too successful at translating vague goals into actions may unintentionally encourage dependency, blunt metacognitive growth, or optimize for short-term fluency over durable learning. This is where the older HCI lineage of mixed-initiative systems is useful: it treats “proactivity” as a negotiable contract—when the system should suggest, when it should ask, and when it should stay quiet—rather than a general virtue (see Horvitz’s framing in [Mixed-Initiative Interaction](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/mixed-initiative-interaction/)). If LAUI is meant to be “much greater” than today’s tool-following agents, Daniel could sharpen the argument by specifying what *rights* the user retains (override, inspect, revert, constrain), and what the agent must disclose (confidence, rationale, alternatives), especially when it is “studying” the user.

Relatedly, the post implies an appealing contrast between “explorable GUI that teaches predefined ways” and “emergent workflow discovered with the agent,” but it underplays what GUIs and pedagogy already contribute: stable mental models, predictable affordances, and learnable constraints. Don Norman’s long-running critique is that good interfaces don’t just *do things for you*; they make it legible what can be done and why it behaves as it does (see [The Design of Everyday Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Design_of_Everyday_Things)). An “ideal LAUI” therefore needs an evaluation target beyond “more proactive”: does it improve learning outcomes, reduce frustration without reducing understanding, and remain reliable under real-time constraints (latency, multimodal errors, hardware noise)? Flute X GPT is a strong testbed precisely because real-time multimodal tutoring forces these questions; the paper would be even more compelling if the LAUI vision explicitly treated “emergent workflow” as something that must remain *auditable and teachable*, not merely discoverable.
